 n.18 (“horizontal restraints are generally less defensible than vertical restraints.”)  
23       Here, the parties dispute whether Defendants entered a “horizontal” agreement, as 
24  Plaintiff argues, or a “vertical” agreement, as Defendants argue. This issue turns on whether 
25  Defendants entered the agreement as “competitors” or “firms at different levels of 
26  distribution.” Bus. Elecs. Corp. v. Sharp Elecs. Corp.,
485 U.S. 717, 730
 (1988). Plaintiff 
1  contends this case is “not about Apple independently selecting its trading partners or Amazon 
2  independently enforcing its own platform rules. It is about two horizontal competitors agreeing 
3  to eliminate the competitive threat posed by hundreds of other horizontal competitors.” (Dkt. No. 
4  37 at 9.) The Court cannot agree with this characterization. See Vasquez,
487 F.3d at 1249
. 
5  According to the facts as pled, “Apple designs, manufactures, and sells iPhones and iPads,” (Dkt. 
6  No. 37 at 12), and Apple “distributes its products through two channels” otherwise known as a 
7  “dual distribution” strategy. (Id.) In the first level, “Apple maintains its own retails stores, 
8  including an online store and physical outlets. This is Apple’s direct distribution channel.” (Id. at 
9  12.) At this level, Apple competes horizontally with other retailers of its products. (Dkt. No. 51 
10  at 21.) In the second level, “Apple distributes its products through a network of third-party 
11  distributors[.]” (Dkt. No. 37 at 12.) In addition to supplying Amazon with products, “Apple 
12  reportedly has Authorized Reseller Agreements with Best Buy, Target, Staples, AT&T, and 
13  others.” (Id. at 13.) At this level, Apple “stands in a vertical relationship with the retailers it 
14  supplies.” (Dkt. No. 51 at 21.)                                           
15       Given these allegations, the Court finds that, although the Defendants may compete for 
16  the sale of products at a horizontal level, they are vertically situated as manufacturer and reseller 
17  under the agreement at issue here. (Dkt. No. 45 at 30.) The GTA provides the conditions for 
18  the sale of Apple products on Amazon’s Marketplace by imposing restrictions on who may sell 
19  Apple products on Amazon’s platform and under what specific circumstances. (Id. at 31.) The 
20  plain text of this agreement strongly suggests that Apple stands as a manufacturer and Amazon 
21  as a distributer in this particular relationship. While the Defendants may be horizontally situated 
22  in other circumstances, this does not automatically place all their dealings—particularly, their 
23  vertical ones—into a per se context.                                      
24       This conclusion is consistent with Ninth Circuit precedent, which holds that the rule of 
25  reason—not the per se standard—typically applies in the context of “dual distribution” 
26  arrangements. See Dimidowich v. Bell & Howell,
803 F.2d 1473, 1481
 (9th Cir. 1986) (The 
1  Ninth Circuit has “categorized restrictions imposed in the context of dual distributorships as 
2  vertical and analyzed them under the rule of reason.”); Frame-Wilson, 591 F. Supp. 3d at 986 
3  (rejecting application of per se standard because relationship at issue was “a vertical arrangement 
4  because it involves different levels of the supply chain.”) To rule otherwise would cut against 
5  well-established precedent protecting the rights and autonomies of manufactures. See, e.g., Krehl 
6  v. Baskin-Robbins Ice Cream Co.,
664 F.2d 1348, 1356-57
 (9th Cir. 1982) (“Competition is 
7  promoted when manufacturers are given wide latitude in establishing their method of distribution 
8  and in choosing particular distributors.”)                                
9       However, the analysis does not end here. Application of the per se rule “must be based 
10  upon demonstrable economic effect rather than . . . upon formalistic line drawing” between the 
11  different types of restraints. Leegin,
551 U.S. at 887
. Plaintiff characterizes the GTA as a “naked 
12  restraint” and urges that prior judicial experience with these categories of restraints requires per 
13  se condemnation of the GTA. (Dkt. No. 37 at 5, 58.) Beyond this conclusory statement, though, 
14  Plaintiff has not made a showing that the restraint at issue is one that “courts have had 
15  considerable experience with,” permitting this Court to “predict with confidence that [the 
16  restraint] would be invalidated in all or almost all instances.” Leegin,
551 U.S. at 886
.  
17       In fact, Plaintiff acknowledges that third-party sellers have not been altogether expelled 
18  from Amazon’s Marketplace—akin to a traditional boycott. (Dkt. No. 51 at 23.) And the fact that 
19  “Apple and Amazon also compete at the retail level is a defining feature of the dual distribution 
20  system, not a fact supporting a pure horizontal agreement requiring the per se rule.” (Dkt. No. 55 
21  at 7.) See Laurence J. Gordon, Inc. v. Brandt, Inc.,
554 F. Supp. 1144, 1152
 (W.D. Wash. 1983). 
22  (explaining that a “finding of [horizontal] competition would not be significant” in light of dual 
23  distribution precedent and rejecting argument that restraint was a “group boycott.”) 
24       Therefore, given the complex nature of the business relationships between the parties and 
25  the challenged restraint at issue—a classic dual-distribution arrangement where a manufacturer 
26  provides its products to a reseller and also competes with that reseller for sales to customers —
1  the Court finds the per se rules to be inapplicable in this case, at least as pleaded. See Leegin, 551 
2  U.S. at 887 (“It should come as no surprise ... that [courts] have ‘expressed reluctance to 
3  adopt per se rules with regard to restraints imposed in the context of business relationships where 
4  the economic impact of certain practices is not immediately obvious.’”)   
5            2.  Rule of Reason                                              
6       Defendants argue the Claim fails to satisfy the rule of reason because the FAC failed (1) 
7  to identify a relevant market; and (2) failed to show anticompetitive effect (injury) in that market. 
8  (Dkt. Nos. 42 at 18–33, 43 at 15–30.) The Court disagrees for the reasons explained below. 
9                 a.  Alleged Marketplace                                    
10       Under the rule of reason Plaintiff must “allege that the defendant has market power 
11  within a ‘relevant market.’” Newcal Indus., Inc. v. Ikon Office Solution,
513 F.3d 1038
, 1044 
12  (9th Cir. 2008). This, by definition, requires sufficient market control that the anticompetitive 
13  conduct actually injures a competitor or consumer.
Id.
 But, at least in an antitrust case, this need 
14  not be pled with specificity.
Id.
 An antitrust complaint survives a Rule 12(b)(6) motion unless it 
15  is apparent from the face of the complaint that the alleged market suffers a fatal legal defect.
Id.
 
16  at 1045. And since the validity of the “relevant market” is typically a factual element rather than 
17  a legal element, alleged markets may survive scrutiny under Rule 12(b)(6), subject to factual 
18  testing by summary judgment or trial. Id.; see also High Tech. Careers v. San Jose Mercury 
19  News,
996 F.2d 987, 990
 (9th Cir. 1993) (holding that “[t]he process of defining the relevant 
20  market is a factual inquiry for the jury.”)                               
21       However, a complaint may be dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6) if the complaint's “relevant 
22  market” definition is facially unsustainable. Newcal,
513 F.3d at 1045
. To avoid dismissal, the 
23  relevant market must be a product market and include the products at issue as well as all 
24  economic substitutes for the products.
Id.
 It must include “the group or groups of sellers or 
25  producers who have actual or potential ability to deprive each other of significant levels of 
26  business.”
Id.
 (quoting Thurman Industries, Inc. v. Pay ‘N Pak Stores, Inc.,
875 F.2d 1369
, 1374 
1  (9th Cir. 1989)).                                                         
2       Here, Plaintiffs identify the market at issue as the two-sided “U.S. Online Marketplace”, 
3  in which Amazon is one player among many. (Dkt. No. 37 at 32, 43.) Within that market, 
4  Plaintiff identifies a submarket for “smartphone transactions.” (Id.) Plaintiff pleads facts to 
5  demonstrate that companies treat smartphones as a “distinct product line.” (Id.) Using similar 
6  logic and facts, Plaintiff also identifies a submarket for “tablet transactions.” (Id.) The Supreme 
7  Court has held that submarkets, “which, in themselves, constitute product markets for antitrust 
8  purposes,” may exist within the broader product market. Brown Shoe Co. v. U.S.,
370 U.S. 294
, 
9  325 (1962.) Submarkets may be determined by “examining such practical indicia as industry or 
10  public recognition of the submarket as a separate economic entity, the product’s peculiar 
11  characteristics and uses, unique production facilities, distinct customers, distinct prices, 
12  sensitivity to price changes, and specialized vendors.”
Id.
 These indicia were not intended “as a 
13  litmus test, and subsequent decisions have made clear that submarkets can exist where only some 
14  of these factors are present.” Bon-Ton Stores, Inc. v. May Dep’t Stores Co.,
881 F. Supp. 860
, 
15  868 (W.D.N.Y. 1994).                                                      
16       Plaintiffs have provided sufficient “practical indicia” to allege, at a minimum, that the 
17  supposed submarkets here are not necessarily facially unsustainable. Plaintiffs allege that the 
18  smartphone and tablet submarkets are publicly recognized as distinct markets within the online 
19  marketplace by consumers and retailers, (Dkt. No. 37 at 34–39), that brick-and-mortar stores are 
20  not a reasonable substitute, (id. at 39), and that Amazon’s marketplace has substantial market 
21  power that reverberates across all online marketplaces, (id. at 46).      
22       Defendant Apple, for its part, argues that Plaintiff’s alleged market is both over-and-
23  under-inclusive. (Dkt. No. 43 at 18–19.) It contends that the alleged market is over-inclusive 
24  because it purports to include “all retail goods” which are neither “reasonably interchangeable 
25  nor have ‘cross-elasticity of demand’ with the iPhones and iPads at issue.” (Id. at 18.) And that it 
26  is under-inclusive because it “fails to capture many other avenues for a customer to purchase 
1  smartphones and tablets.” (Id. at 19.) The Court is unpersuaded.          
2       Plaintiff has alleged sufficient facts to (1) demonstrate why the proffered submarkets do 
3  not exclude any reasonable substitutes, (Dkt. No. 37 at 18), and (2) to support a distinction 
4  between the submarkets for iPhones and iPads and the rest of the goods sold on online 
5  marketplaces, (id.), even though the same products may be available in both. See F.T.C. v. Whole 
6  Foods Mkt., Inc.,
548 F.3d 1028, 1040
 (D.C. Cir. 2008) (holding that premium natural and 
7  organic supermarkets may constitute a submarket distinct from conventional supermarkets even 
8  if some of the products were available in both markets). As the court in Whole Foods explained, 
9  “[t]he fact that a customer might buy a stick of gum at a supermarket or at a convenience store 
10  does not mean there is no definable groceries market.”
Id.
                
11       Finding no “fatal legal defect,” the Court cannot conclude, as Defendants argue, that the 
12  “relevant market” here is facially unsustainable. Hicks, 897 F.3d at 1120. Both Defendants 
13  dispute the facts as pled in the FAC, but the validity of the relevant market is a question reserved 
14  for a jury, and the Court makes no such determination here. Newcal,
513 F.3d at 1045
; see also 
15  GTE Corp., 692 F.3d at 790 (holding that “[d]efining the relevant market is a factual inquiry 
16  ordinarily reserved for the jury.”).                                      
17                 b.  Alleged Injury                                         
18       Defendants further argue that Plaintiff failed to show injury to self and/or anticompetitive 
19  effect. (Dkt. Nos. 42 at 26, 43 at 24.) “A plaintiff may only pursue an antitrust action if it can 
20  show antitrust injury, which is to say injury of the type the antitrust laws were intended to 
21  prevent and that flows from that which makes defendants’ acts unlawful.” Am. Ad Mgmt., Inc. v. 
22  Gen. Tel. Co. of California,
190 F.3d 1051, 1055
 (9th Cir. 1999) (internal citations omitted). 
23       According to the FAC, Plaintiff purchased an Apple iPad on the Amazon Marketplace, 
24  and, but for the GTA, he would have “paid a lower price.” (Dkt. No. 37 at 12.) Plaintiff claims 
25  the GTA “eliminated competitive resellers of Apple products” and “those eliminated sellers 
26  would have would have caused prices for these products, including the Apple iPad purchased by 
1  Plaintiff, to be lower.” (Id.) Plaintiff has also pled facts to show the GTA had anticompetitive 
2  effects on the merchant side of the market, (id. at 24); on the consumer side of the market, (id. at 
3  25); and that it reduced output, (id. at 28). This combined to benefit Defendants, (id. at 29), and 
4  harm consumers, (id. at 30). While Defendants assert the GTA, and its subsequent effects, are the 
5  result of pro-competitive and anti-counterfeit motivations, (Dkt. No. 42 at 26, 43 at 24), the 
6  Court will cannot address that countervailing fact at this time. See SmileCare Dental Group v. 
7  Delta Dental Plan of California,
88 F.3d 780, 783
 (9th Cir. 1996) (holding that “[d]ismissal for 
8  failure to state a claim is appropriate where the complaint states no set of facts which, if true, 
9  would constitute an antitrust offense, notwithstanding its conclusory language regarding the 
10  elimination of competition and improper purpose.”)                        
11       Accordingly, the Court finds that, based on an application of the rule of reason, the facts 
12  as alleged would constitute an offense—regardless of how Defendants would prefer to frame 
13  them—and that they are sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss.         
14  III.  CONCLUSION                                                          
15       For the foregoing reasons, Defendants’ motions to dismiss (Dkt. Nos. 42, 43) are 
16  DENIED in part and GRANTED in part. The Court DENIES Defendants’ motions to dismiss 
17  under a rule of reason analysis. The Court GRANTS Defendant’s motions to dismiss Plaintiff’s 
18  claim under a per se analysis with prejudice.

12                                                                             
         This matter comes before the Court on a motion for leave to amend the complaint, filed by 
13                                                                             
    Plaintiff’s class counsel.  Dkt. No. 80.  The Court has considered the parties’ briefing,1 the oral 
14                                                                             
    argument of counsel, and the remainder of the record.  For the reasons explained herein, the Court 
15                                                                             
    grants the motion for leave to amend.                                     
16                                                                             
                            I.  BACKGROUND                                    
17                                                                             
         Plaintiff Steven Floyd filed this putative class action in November 2022, alleging that the 
18                                                                             
    Global Tenets Agreement between Defendants Apple Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. violates Section 
19                                                                             
    1 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1.  Dkt. No. 1.  Defendants filed motions to dismiss in February 
20                                                                             
    2023 (Dkt. Nos. 30, 32), and Floyd filed an amended complaint in response (Dkt. No. 37).  
21                                                                             
    Defendants filed another round of motions to dismiss in March 2023 (Dkt. Nos. 42, 43), which 
22                                                                             
    were granted in part and denied in part in June 2023.  See Dkt. No. 61.   
23                                                                             

24   1 This order refers to the parties’ briefing using the CM/ECF page numbers. 
1        Since then, the parties have worked to resolve discovery-related disputes, some of which 
2   have warranted Court intervention.  See Dkt. Nos. 53, 70, 74, 77.  In February 2024, class counsel 
3   filed a motion to amend the complaint to add class representatives because Floyd “recently ceased 

4   responding to inquiries from counsel for the proposed class[.]”  Dkt. No. 80 at 5.  The motion 
5   proposes  amending  the  complaint  to  list  Jolene  Furdek  and  Jonathan  Ryan  as  new  class 
6   representatives asserting the same Sherman Act claim, on the same facts alleged in the first 
7   amended  complaint.    Id.;  Dkt.  No.  81-4.  The proposed  amended  complaint  also  omits  the 
8   allegations that were dismissed in the order granting in part the motions to dismiss, without 
9   waiving the right to challenge the dismissal on appeal.  See Dkt. No. 81-4 at 14 n.15.   
10        Defendants oppose the motion for leave to amend on a variety of grounds (Dkt. No. 86), 
11   but for the following reasons, the Court grants the motion.               
12                             II.  ANALYSIS                                   

13   A.   Legal Standards                                                      
14        A party may amend its pleading once as a matter of course, and thereafter “only with the 
15   opposing party’s written consent or the court’s leave.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2).  “The court should 
16   freely give leave when justice so requires.”  Id.  A court “considers the following five factors to 
17   assess whether to grant leave to amend: (1) bad faith, (2) undue delay, (3) prejudice to the opposing 
18   party, (4) futility of amendment; and (5) whether plaintiff has previously amended his complaint.”  
19   In re W. States Wholesale Nat. Gas Antitrust Litig., 715 F.3d 716, 738 (9th Cir. 2013) (cleaned 
20   up), aff’d sub nom. Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373 (2015).  “The opposing party bears 
21   the burden to show why leave to amend should not be granted.”  Robertson v. Bruckert, 568 F. 
22   Supp. 3d 1044, 1047 (N.D. Cal. 2021).                                     

23        If a court’s scheduling order sets forth a deadline for amending the pleadings, no post-
24   deadline amendment is permitted unless the court first finds good cause to amend the case 
1   schedule.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(4); Kamal v. Eden Creamery, LLC, 88 F.4th 1268, 1277 (9th 
2   Cir. 2023).  Good cause exists where the moving party is diligent in requesting a modification.  
3   Johnson v. Mammoth Recreations, Inc., 975 F.2d 604, 607–09 (9th Cir. 1992).   

4        “Although the existence or degree of prejudice to the party opposing the modification 
5   might supply additional reasons to deny a motion [for leave to amend], the focus of the inquiry is 
6   upon the moving party’s reasons for seeking modification,” and “[i]f that party was not diligent, 
7   the inquiry should end.”  Johnson, 975 F.2d at 609.                       
8        To demonstrate diligence under Rule 16’s “good cause” standard, the movant may 
         be required to show the following: (1) that he was diligent in assisting the court in 
9        creating a workable Rule 16 order; (2) that his noncompliance with a Rule 16 
         deadline occurred or will occur, notwithstanding his diligent efforts to comply, 
10        because of the development of matters which could not have been reasonably 
         foreseen or anticipated at the time of the Rule 16 scheduling conference; and (3) 
11        that he was diligent in seeking amendment of the Rule 16 order, once it became 
         apparent that he could not comply with the order.                    
12                                                                             
    Morgal v. Maricopa Cnty. Bd. of Supervisors, 284 F.R.D. 452, 460 (D. Ariz. 2012) (cleaned up).  
13                                                                             
    “Only after the moving party has demonstrated diligence under Rule 16 does the court apply the 
14                                                                             
    standard under Rule 15 to determine whether the amendment [is] proper.”  Hood v. Hartford Life 
15                                                                             
    & Accident Ins. Co., 567 F. Supp. 2d 1221, 1224 (E.D. Cal. 2008).         
16                                                                             
         “To permit a party to disregard a Rule 16 order by an appeal to the standards of Rule 
17                                                                             
    15 would ‘undermine the court’s ability to control its docket, disrupt the agreed-upon course of 
18                                                                             
    the litigation, and reward the indolent and the cavalier.’”  Eckert Cold Storage, Inc. v. Behl, 943 
19                                                                             
    F. Supp. 1230, 1233 (E.D. Cal. 1996) (quoting Johnson, 975 F.2d at 610–11).  A determination of 
20                                                                             
    whether good cause exists to modify a case schedule is committed to the broad discretion of the 
21                                                                             
    district court.  See C.F. ex rel. Farman v. Capistrano Unified Sch. Dist., 654 F.3d 975, 984 (9th 
22                                                                             
    Cir. 2011).                                                               
23                                                                             

24                                                                             
1   B.   Adjudication of Plaintiff’s Adequacy as a Class Representative is Premature. 

2        Before turning to consider the motion for leave to amend under the applicable Federal 
3   Rules of Civil Procedure, the Court first addresses Defendants’ primary argument in opposition, 
4   which is that Floyd is an inadequate named Plaintiff.  Specifically, Defendants argue that because 
5   Floyd was never qualified to represent the class in the first place, “[s]ubjecting Defendants to the 
6   burdens of litigation for over a year with a plaintiff who is an inadequate representative of the 
7   putative class, while simultaneously refusing to produce documents or offer dates for deposition, 
8   is conduct that makes amendment inappropriate.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 10.  According to Defendants, 
9   the motion to amend is not simply a motion to add or substitute a class representative, but should 
10   be considered a “back-door attempt to begin the action anew.”  Id. (quoting Lidie v. State of Cal., 
11   478 F.2d 552, 555 (9th Cir. 1973)).                                       
12        But whether Floyd is an adequate representative of the putative class is not before the Court 

13   at this point in the litigation, and Defendants will have an opportunity to fully litigate this issue in 
14   the context of a motion for class certification.  Defendants have not shown that Floyd’s potential 
15   inadequacy as a class representative is an inherent defect in his party status akin to a lack of 
16   standing or mootness, such that there is no live case or controversy before the Court.  In the absence 
17   of an inherent defect in Floyd’s claims, the Court will allow amendment of the complaint to add 
18   additional named plaintiffs.  See, e.g., Kirby v. McMenamins Inc., C22-5168-BHS-MLP, 2023 WL 
19   4623988 (W.D. Wash. July 19, 2023); Fife v. Sci. Games Corp., No. 2:18-cv-00565-RBL, 2020 
20   WL 4933959, at *1–2 (W.D. Wash. Aug. 24, 2020) (finding that a putative class action is not 
21   mooted when a sole named plaintiff seeks to withdraw for personal reasons but can be replaced 
22   immediately); Castillo v. United Rentals (N. Am.), Inc., No. C17-1573JLR, 2018 WL 3429936, at 

23   *3 (W.D. Wash. July 16, 2018) (permitting a pre-certification substitution of the named plaintiff 
24                                                                             
1   where the current sole named plaintiff’s claims persist (had not been settled or dismissed), and 
2   counsel could produce a substitute immediately).                          
3        The absence of an adjudication of Floyd’s adequacy distinguishes this case from cases cited 

4   by Defendants.  For example, Defendants rely on Lidie, 478 F.2d at 555, where the Ninth Circuit 
5   upheld a denial of a motion to intervene because, “where the original plaintiffs were never qualified 
6   to represent the class, a motion to intervene represents a back-door attempt to begin the action 
7   anew, and need not be granted.”  But here, Floyd has not been found unqualified to represent the 
8   putative  class.    Although  Defendants  vigorously  dispute  Floyd’s  adequacy  as  a  class 
9   representative, the Court finds that it would be premature to adjudicate this issue in the context of 
10   a motion for leave to amend.                                              
11        Likewise, Defendants ask the Court to follow Miller v. Mercedes-Benz USA LLC, No. CV 
12   06-0532 ABC (JTLX), 2009 WL 1393488, at *1–2 (C.D. Cal. May 15, 2009), but in that case, the 

13   sole named plaintiff included in her motion for class certification a request to add an additional 
14   named plaintiff to cure her own conflict of interest in serving as a class representative.  The Miller 
15   court denied the current named plaintiff’s motion for class certification because she could not fairly 
16   and adequately protect the interests of the class, and found that her last-minute attempt to add a 
17   named plaintiff was a “bait-and-switch tactic.”  Id. at *2.  Miller is distinguishable from this case 
18   because the motion before that court requested class certification, which required the court to 
19   determine whether the sole named plaintiff was an adequate representative.  This case has not 
20   proceeded to that stage of litigation, and the Court declines to consider issues now, on this record 
21   and with limited briefing, that it will have the opportunity to consider in full at class certification. 
22   C.   There is Good Cause to Amend the Case Schedule.                      

23        The Court now considers whether the motion for leave to amend should be granted under 
24   the applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.  First, the Court must resolve the parties’ dispute 
1   as  to  whether  Rule  15  (addressing  leave  to  amend  pleadings)  and/or  Rule  16  (addressing 
2   modifications to a case schedule) applies to the motion.                  
3        Here, the case schedule does not set out a deadline for either amending pleadings or adding 

4   parties, but sets deadlines only as to substantial completion of productions, fact discovery cutoff, 
5   disclosure of expert reports, and the briefing of a class-certification motion.  See Dkt. No. 68.  
6   Although the motion for leave to amend the complaint is therefore not technically untimely under 
7   this case schedule, Defendants nonetheless contend that the motion for leave to amend should be 
8   considered under Rule 16 because granting it would necessitate modifying the scheduling order: 
9   the deadlines for substantial completion of productions (April 3, 2024) and the fact discovery 
10   cutoff (July 8, 2024) cannot be met if the complaint is amended.  Dkt. No. 86 at 12.  Defendants 
11   argue that even if class counsel agrees to treat all discovery requests on Floyd as if they had been 
12   served on the new representatives, as counsel has offered, Defendants would still want to serve 

13   discovery requests tailored to the new representatives, and they would not have been able to 
14   respond to those requests by April 3.  Id.                                
15        Indeed, while the motion for leave to amend was pending, the parties filed a stipulated 
16   motion to suspend the April 3 deadline and indicated that they will confer regarding a new case 
17   schedule after the Court has resolved all motions currently pending.  See Dkt. No. 93.  Under these 
18   circumstances, where even the filing of a motion for leave to amend has necessitated adjustment 
19   of the case schedule, the Court finds that Rule 16 applies and good cause must be shown to modify 
20   the case schedule, before the Court will consider whether the motion for leave to amend should be 
21   granted under Rule 15.  See Paz v. City of Aberdeen, No. C13-5104 RJB, 2013 WL 6163016, at 
22   *2–3 (W.D. Wash. Nov. 25, 2013).                                          

23        The good cause standard has been easily met here.  Class counsel diligently moved to 
24   substitute the new representatives after Floyd unexpectedly stopped communicating with them.  
1   Counsel last communicated with Floyd on January 16, 2024 (Dkt. No. 81-1 at 2) and moved to 
2   amend the complaint on February 29, 2024.  Dkt. No. 80.  That span of time reflects diligence.  
3   See, e.g., Kirby, 2023 WL 4623988, at *4 (finding that counsel had been diligent in bringing the 

4   motion for leave to amend less than two months after receiving contact information for putative 
5   class members and less than a month after the new class representatives expressed interest in 
6   becoming class representatives and retained counsel).  Moreover, amendment permits this case to 
7   move forward after Floyd apparently lost interest in continuing to participate, which constitutes 
8   good cause for amendment.  See Fife, 2020 WL 4933959, at *3.              
9        Defendants suggest that counsel was not diligent in selecting Floyd as a named plaintiff in 
10   the first place, because counsel should have known from this case’s inception (or at least since the 
11   motions to dismiss were granted in part) that Floyd does not adequately represent the class due to 
12   his shopping behavior.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14–15.  Accepting this argument would require the Court 

13   to consider Floyd’s adequacy as a class representative prematurely.  Again, Floyd’s adequacy as a 
14   class representative has not been adjudicated to date and will not be adjudicated on an incomplete 
15   record in the context of this motion.                                     
16   D.   Justice Requires Leave to Amend the Complaint.                       

17        The Court has found good cause to amend the case schedule, and now turns to consider 
18   whether the motion for leave to amend the complaint should be granted under Rule 15.  As noted 
19   above, Defendants bear the burden of showing that justice requires denying the motion for leave 
20   to amend.  Defendants contend that the motion should be denied in light of undue delay and 
21   prejudice, but for the following reasons, the Court disagrees.            
22        1.  Undue Delay                                                      
23        First, Defendants argue that class counsel unduly delayed in seeking amendment because 
24   they should have known earlier that Floyd was an inadequate class representative.  Dkt. No. 86 at 
1   14–15.  As stated supra, that is not the grounds upon which amendment is requested, and the Court 
2   will not assume Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative simply because Defendants assert it, 
3   nor will the Court adjudicate that issue without the benefit of full briefing.  Because Defendants 

4   have not identified a point in this litigation where Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative was 
5   made plain to class counsel, the Court will not start the diligence clock running at a point earlier 
6   than the time when Floyd stopped communicating with counsel.  And for the reasons stated supra 
7   with respect to Rule 16, and the Court finds that counsel was diligent in filing this motion after 
8   that time.                                                                
9        2.  Prejudice                                                        
10        Second, Defendants argue that they would be prejudiced via the need to conduct new and/or 
11   additional discovery that would not otherwise have been required had class counsel identified the 
12   appropriate representatives in the first instance.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14.  Given that the parties have 

13   recently agreed to suspend the discovery deadlines and discovery has not even closed under the 
14   original  deadlines,  Defendants  have  not  shown  that  permitting  amendment  would  lead  to 
15   substantial prejudice.  The cases Defendants cite to support a finding of undue prejudice involve 
16   amendments sought after discovery had closed or after a motion for class certification was filed.  
17   See Paz, 2013 WL 6163016, at *4; In re Flash Memory Antitrust Litig., No. C 07-0086 SBA, 2010 
18   WL 2332081, at *17 (N.D. Cal. June 9, 2010).                              
19        Defendants also argue that the amendments are intended to “circumvent a potentially fatal 
20   statute of limitations issue” and that Defendants “would be prejudiced by having to defend against 
21   an untimely putative class action.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 13.  Defendants state that they did not raise this 
22   issue in their motions to dismiss because resolving it requires deposing Floyd.  Id. at 13 n.3.  But 

23   this issue is not squarely before the Court, and has not been briefed, given that Floyd has not yet 
24   been deposed.  The Court again declines to wade into substantive issues prematurely, without the 
1   benefit of full briefing and an adequate record, and the Court cannot find that Defendants are 
2   prejudiced by having to defend this case while its timeliness is still an open question. 
3        For all of these reasons, the Court finds that the motion for leave to amend is supported by 

4   good cause and that Defendants have not shown that justice requires its denial.  Because leave to 
5   amend the complaint is granted, the motion to intervene in the alternative (Dkt. No. 80 at 14–16) 
6   is denied as moot.                                                        
7   E.   The Parties Shall Confer Regarding a New Case Schedule.              
8        Defendants request that if the Court grants leave to amend, the Court should also  
9        stay discovery as to the Defendants for 90 days (and suspend the extant substantial 
         completion deadline) to further the just and efficient resolution of this case.…  This 
10        will allow Defendants to take initial discovery of the new  representatives to 
         determine if there is even a viable plaintiff in this case, and to establish amendment 
11        would  not  be  futile.    After  the  new  representatives  (or  Floyd)  meet  their 
         corresponding discovery obligations, then Defendants should have the opportunity 
12        to file a dispositive motion or continue with discovery on a revised schedule. 

13   Dkt. No. 86 at 16.  Class counsel’s reply objects to a discovery stay that would apply to Defendants 
14   only, noting that Defendants “have not produced a single responsive document” to date.  Dkt. No. 
15   92 at 10.                                                                 
16        As noted supra, after Defendants’ opposition to the motion for leave to amend was filed, 
17   the parties filed a stipulated motion to suspend the case schedule until after the Court resolved the 
18   pending motions.  See Dkt. No. 93.  The parties agreed that they would confer regarding a new 
19   case schedule and, if necessary, set out a briefing schedule on a contested motion to modify the 
20   schedule.  Id.  Thus, at this time, the Court finds that Defendants’ concern in their opposition 
21   regarding the case schedule has been mooted by the subsequent stipulation.  Defendants will have 
22   an opportunity to address any concerns about schedule revisions either when conferring with class 
23   counsel or when briefing a contested motion to modify the case schedule, if one is necessary. 
24   //                                                                        
1                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  
2        For these reasons, the Court GRANTS the motion for leave to amend.  Dkt. No. 80.  A 
3   second amended complaint shall be filed no later than May 10, 2024.       

4        The parties shall confer regarding case schedule modification and whether the statement of 
5   discovery disputes filed on March 26, 2024 (Dkt. No. 90) should be re-briefed in light of this order.  
6   The parties shall file either a stipulation on these issues or set forth a briefing schedule on these 
7   issues, no later than May 13, 2024.  The clerk is directed to terminate the dispute (Dkt. No. 90) at 
8   this time, subject to reactivation by the Court after reviewing the parties’ submission. 
9        Plaintiffs are also granted leave to file a motion to compel with regard to the disputes 
10   outlined in the joint statement filed on March 22, 2024.  Dkt. No. 89.  As discussed at the discovery 
11   conference, the Court finds that the issues to be resolved in that statement of disputes warrants full 
12   briefing.  The clerk is directed to terminate the dispute (Dkt. No. 89) as a motion at this time.   

13        Dated this 6th day of May, 2024.

975 F.2d at 609
.                       
8        To demonstrate diligence under Rule 16’s “good cause” standard, the movant may 
         be required to show the following: (1) that he was diligent in assisting the court in 
9        creating a workable Rule 16 order; (2) that his noncompliance with a Rule 16 
         deadline occurred or will occur, notwithstanding his diligent efforts to comply, 
10        because of the development of matters which could not have been reasonably 
         foreseen or anticipated at the time of the Rule 16 scheduling conference; and (3) 
11        that he was diligent in seeking amendment of the Rule 16 order, once it became 
         apparent that he could not comply with the order.                    
12                                                                             
    Morgal v. Maricopa Cnty. Bd. of Supervisors,
284 F.R.D. 452, 460
 (D. Ariz. 2012) (cleaned up).  
13                                                                             
    “Only after the moving party has demonstrated diligence under Rule 16 does the court apply the 
14                                                                             
    standard under Rule 15 to determine whether the amendment [is] proper.”  Hood v. Hartford Life 
15                                                                             
    & Accident Ins. Co.,
567 F. Supp. 2d 1221, 1224
 (E.D. Cal. 2008).         
16                                                                             
         “To permit a party to disregard a Rule 16 order by an appeal to the standards of Rule 
17                                                                             
    15 would ‘undermine the court’s ability to control its docket, disrupt the agreed-upon course of 
18                                                                             
    the litigation, and reward the indolent and the cavalier.’”  Eckert Cold Storage, Inc. v. Behl, 943
19 F. Supp. 1230
, 1233 (E.D. Cal. 1996) (quoting Johnson, 975 F.2d at 610–11).  A determination of 
20                                                                             
    whether good cause exists to modify a case schedule is committed to the broad discretion of the 
21                                                                             
    district court.  See C.F. ex rel. Farman v. Capistrano Unified Sch. Dist.,
654 F.3d 975, 984
 (9th 
22                                                                             
    Cir. 2011).                                                               
23                                                                             

24                                                                             
1   B.   Adjudication of Plaintiff’s Adequacy as a Class Representative is Premature. 

2        Before turning to consider the motion for leave to amend under the applicable Federal 
3   Rules of Civil Procedure, the Court first addresses Defendants’ primary argument in opposition, 
4   which is that Floyd is an inadequate named Plaintiff.  Specifically, Defendants argue that because 
5   Floyd was never qualified to represent the class in the first place, “[s]ubjecting Defendants to the 
6   burdens of litigation for over a year with a plaintiff who is an inadequate representative of the 
7   putative class, while simultaneously refusing to produce documents or offer dates for deposition, 
8   is conduct that makes amendment inappropriate.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 10.  According to Defendants, 
9   the motion to amend is not simply a motion to add or substitute a class representative, but should 
10   be considered a “back-door attempt to begin the action anew.”
Id.
 (quoting Lidie v. State of Cal., 
11
478 F.2d 552, 555
 (9th Cir. 1973)).                                       
12        But whether Floyd is an adequate representative of the putative class is not before the Court 

13   at this point in the litigation, and Defendants will have an opportunity to fully litigate this issue in 
14   the context of a motion for class certification.  Defendants have not shown that Floyd’s potential 
15   inadequacy as a class representative is an inherent defect in his party status akin to a lack of 
16   standing or mootness, such that there is no live case or controversy before the Court.  In the absence 
17   of an inherent defect in Floyd’s claims, the Court will allow amendment of the complaint to add 
18   additional named plaintiffs.  See, e.g., Kirby v. McMenamins Inc., C22-5168-BHS-MLP,
2023 WL 19
   4623988 (W.D. Wash. July 19, 2023); Fife v. Sci. Games Corp., No. 2:18-cv-00565-RBL, 2020
20 WL 4933959
, at *1–2 (W.D. Wash. Aug. 24, 2020) (finding that a putative class action is not 
21   mooted when a sole named plaintiff seeks to withdraw for personal reasons but can be replaced 
22   immediately); Castillo v. United Rentals (N. Am.), Inc., No. C17-1573JLR,
2018 WL 3429936
, at 

23   *3 (W.D. Wash. July 16, 2018) (permitting a pre-certification substitution of the named plaintiff 
24                                                                             
1   where the current sole named plaintiff’s claims persist (had not been settled or dismissed), and 
2   counsel could produce a substitute immediately).                          
3        The absence of an adjudication of Floyd’s adequacy distinguishes this case from cases cited 

4   by Defendants.  For example, Defendants rely on Lidie,
478 F.2d at 555
, where the Ninth Circuit 
5   upheld a denial of a motion to intervene because, “where the original plaintiffs were never qualified 
6   to represent the class, a motion to intervene represents a back-door attempt to begin the action 
7   anew, and need not be granted.”  But here, Floyd has not been found unqualified to represent the 
8   putative  class.    Although  Defendants  vigorously  dispute  Floyd’s  adequacy  as  a  class 
9   representative, the Court finds that it would be premature to adjudicate this issue in the context of 
10   a motion for leave to amend.                                              
11        Likewise, Defendants ask the Court to follow Miller v. Mercedes-Benz USA LLC, No. CV 
12   06-0532 ABC (JTLX),
2009 WL 1393488
, at *1–2 (C.D. Cal. May 15, 2009), but in that case, the 

13   sole named plaintiff included in her motion for class certification a request to add an additional 
14   named plaintiff to cure her own conflict of interest in serving as a class representative.  The Miller 
15   court denied the current named plaintiff’s motion for class certification because she could not fairly 
16   and adequately protect the interests of the class, and found that her last-minute attempt to add a 
17   named plaintiff was a “bait-and-switch tactic.”
Id. at *2
.  Miller is distinguishable from this case 
18   because the motion before that court requested class certification, which required the court to 
19   determine whether the sole named plaintiff was an adequate representative.  This case has not 
20   proceeded to that stage of litigation, and the Court declines to consider issues now, on this record 
21   and with limited briefing, that it will have the opportunity to consider in full at class certification. 
22   C.   There is Good Cause to Amend the Case Schedule.                      

23        The Court now considers whether the motion for leave to amend should be granted under 
24   the applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.  First, the Court must resolve the parties’ dispute 
1   as  to  whether  Rule  15  (addressing  leave  to  amend  pleadings)  and/or  Rule  16  (addressing 
2   modifications to a case schedule) applies to the motion.                  
3        Here, the case schedule does not set out a deadline for either amending pleadings or adding 

4   parties, but sets deadlines only as to substantial completion of productions, fact discovery cutoff, 
5   disclosure of expert reports, and the briefing of a class-certification motion.  See Dkt. No. 68.  
6   Although the motion for leave to amend the complaint is therefore not technically untimely under 
7   this case schedule, Defendants nonetheless contend that the motion for leave to amend should be 
8   considered under Rule 16 because granting it would necessitate modifying the scheduling order: 
9   the deadlines for substantial completion of productions (April 3, 2024) and the fact discovery 
10   cutoff (July 8, 2024) cannot be met if the complaint is amended.  Dkt. No. 86 at 12.  Defendants 
11   argue that even if class counsel agrees to treat all discovery requests on Floyd as if they had been 
12   served on the new representatives, as counsel has offered, Defendants would still want to serve 

13   discovery requests tailored to the new representatives, and they would not have been able to 
14   respond to those requests by April 3.
Id.
                                
15        Indeed, while the motion for leave to amend was pending, the parties filed a stipulated 
16   motion to suspend the April 3 deadline and indicated that they will confer regarding a new case 
17   schedule after the Court has resolved all motions currently pending.  See Dkt. No. 93.  Under these 
18   circumstances, where even the filing of a motion for leave to amend has necessitated adjustment 
19   of the case schedule, the Court finds that Rule 16 applies and good cause must be shown to modify 
20   the case schedule, before the Court will consider whether the motion for leave to amend should be 
21   granted under Rule 15.  See Paz v. City of Aberdeen, No. C13-5104 RJB,
2013 WL 6163016
, at 
22   *2–3 (W.D. Wash. Nov. 25, 2013).                                          

23        The good cause standard has been easily met here.  Class counsel diligently moved to 
24   substitute the new representatives after Floyd unexpectedly stopped communicating with them.  
1   Counsel last communicated with Floyd on January 16, 2024 (Dkt. No. 81-1 at 2) and moved to 
2   amend the complaint on February 29, 2024.  Dkt. No. 80.  That span of time reflects diligence.  
3   See, e.g., Kirby,
2023 WL 4623988
, at *4 (finding that counsel had been diligent in bringing the 

4   motion for leave to amend less than two months after receiving contact information for putative 
5   class members and less than a month after the new class representatives expressed interest in 
6   becoming class representatives and retained counsel).  Moreover, amendment permits this case to 
7   move forward after Floyd apparently lost interest in continuing to participate, which constitutes 
8   good cause for amendment.  See Fife,
2020 WL 4933959
, at *3.              
9        Defendants suggest that counsel was not diligent in selecting Floyd as a named plaintiff in 
10   the first place, because counsel should have known from this case’s inception (or at least since the 
11   motions to dismiss were granted in part) that Floyd does not adequately represent the class due to 
12   his shopping behavior.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14–15.  Accepting this argument would require the Court 

13   to consider Floyd’s adequacy as a class representative prematurely.  Again, Floyd’s adequacy as a 
14   class representative has not been adjudicated to date and will not be adjudicated on an incomplete 
15   record in the context of this motion.                                     
16   D.   Justice Requires Leave to Amend the Complaint.                       

17        The Court has found good cause to amend the case schedule, and now turns to consider 
18   whether the motion for leave to amend the complaint should be granted under Rule 15.  As noted 
19   above, Defendants bear the burden of showing that justice requires denying the motion for leave 
20   to amend.  Defendants contend that the motion should be denied in light of undue delay and 
21   prejudice, but for the following reasons, the Court disagrees.            
22        1.  Undue Delay                                                      
23        First, Defendants argue that class counsel unduly delayed in seeking amendment because 
24   they should have known earlier that Floyd was an inadequate class representative.  Dkt. No. 86 at 
1   14–15.  As stated supra, that is not the grounds upon which amendment is requested, and the Court 
2   will not assume Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative simply because Defendants assert it, 
3   nor will the Court adjudicate that issue without the benefit of full briefing.  Because Defendants 

4   have not identified a point in this litigation where Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative was 
5   made plain to class counsel, the Court will not start the diligence clock running at a point earlier 
6   than the time when Floyd stopped communicating with counsel.  And for the reasons stated supra 
7   with respect to Rule 16, and the Court finds that counsel was diligent in filing this motion after 
8   that time.                                                                
9        2.  Prejudice                                                        
10        Second, Defendants argue that they would be prejudiced via the need to conduct new and/or 
11   additional discovery that would not otherwise have been required had class counsel identified the 
12   appropriate representatives in the first instance.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14.  Given that the parties have 

13   recently agreed to suspend the discovery deadlines and discovery has not even closed under the 
14   original  deadlines,  Defendants  have  not  shown  that  permitting  amendment  would  lead  to 
15   substantial prejudice.  The cases Defendants cite to support a finding of undue prejudice involve 
16   amendments sought after discovery had closed or after a motion for class certification was filed.  
17   See Paz,
2013 WL 6163016
, at *4; In re Flash Memory Antitrust Litig., No. C 07-0086 SBA, 2010
18 WL 2332081
, at *17 (N.D. Cal. June 9, 2010).                              
19        Defendants also argue that the amendments are intended to “circumvent a potentially fatal 
20   statute of limitations issue” and that Defendants “would be prejudiced by having to defend against 
21   an untimely putative class action.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 13.  Defendants state that they did not raise this 
22   issue in their motions to dismiss because resolving it requires deposing Floyd.
Id.
 at 13 n.3.  But 

23   this issue is not squarely before the Court, and has not been briefed, given that Floyd has not yet 
24   been deposed.  The Court again declines to wade into substantive issues prematurely, without the 
1   benefit of full briefing and an adequate record, and the Court cannot find that Defendants are 
2   prejudiced by having to defend this case while its timeliness is still an open question. 
3        For all of these reasons, the Court finds that the motion for leave to amend is supported by 

4   good cause and that Defendants have not shown that justice requires its denial.  Because leave to 
5   amend the complaint is granted, the motion to intervene in the alternative (Dkt. No. 80 at 14–16) 
6   is denied as moot.                                                        
7   E.   The Parties Shall Confer Regarding a New Case Schedule.              
8        Defendants request that if the Court grants leave to amend, the Court should also  
9        stay discovery as to the Defendants for 90 days (and suspend the extant substantial 
         completion deadline) to further the just and efficient resolution of this case.…  This 
10        will allow Defendants to take initial discovery of the new  representatives to 
         determine if there is even a viable plaintiff in this case, and to establish amendment 
11        would  not  be  futile.    After  the  new  representatives  (or  Floyd)  meet  their 
         corresponding discovery obligations, then Defendants should have the opportunity 
12        to file a dispositive motion or continue with discovery on a revised schedule. 

13   Dkt. No. 86 at 16.  Class counsel’s reply objects to a discovery stay that would apply to Defendants 
14   only, noting that Defendants “have not produced a single responsive document” to date.  Dkt. No. 
15   92 at 10.                                                                 
16        As noted supra, after Defendants’ opposition to the motion for leave to amend was filed, 
17   the parties filed a stipulated motion to suspend the case schedule until after the Court resolved the 
18   pending motions.  See Dkt. No. 93.  The parties agreed that they would confer regarding a new 
19   case schedule and, if necessary, set out a briefing schedule on a contested motion to modify the 
20   schedule.  Id.  Thus, at this time, the Court finds that Defendants’ concern in their opposition 
21   regarding the case schedule has been mooted by the subsequent stipulation.  Defendants will have 
22   an opportunity to address any concerns about schedule revisions either when conferring with class 
23   counsel or when briefing a contested motion to modify the case schedule, if one is necessary. 
24   //                                                                        
1                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  
2        For these reasons, the Court GRANTS the motion for leave to amend.  Dkt. No. 80.  A 
3   second amended complaint shall be filed no later than May 10, 2024.       

4        The parties shall confer regarding case schedule modification and whether the statement of 
5   discovery disputes filed on March 26, 2024 (Dkt. No. 90) should be re-briefed in light of this order.

1                         I.   BACKGROUND                                     
2        This case was filed in November 2022 as a putative class action with Floyd as the sole 
3   named plaintiff, alleging that he was overcharged when he purchased a new Apple product on 

4   Amazon’s website as a result of the Global Tenets Agreement between Defendants.  See, e.g., Dkt. 
5   No. 1 ¶ 22.  Since the time of filing, the parties have briefed two rounds of motions to dismiss, a 
6   contested  motion  to  amend  the  complaint,  and  several  discovery  disputes  requiring  Court 
7   intervention.  Dkt. Nos. 30, 32, 42, 43, 53, 76, 80, 89, 90.              
8        Defendants served requests for production on Floyd, and his counsel objected on multiple 
9   general and specific grounds in October 2023.  See Dkt. No. 90 at 31–75.  Floyd has not produced 
10   any documents in response to those requests (or any others).  Dkt. No. 104 at 6.  On February 8, 
11   2024, Apple served interrogatories on Floyd, seeking information about his purchases and use of 
12   smartphones and tablets, as well as the purchases and uses of his household members.  Dkt. No. 

13   90 at 10.  On February 13, Floyd’s counsel responded to Apple, explaining that Floyd had “become 
14   difficult to reach” but had “not withdrawn as a class representative[.]”  Dkt. No. 105 at 6.  
15   Defendants replied on February 22, inquiring as to (among other things) Floyd’s availability for a 
16   deposition.  Id. at 5.  His counsel responded the next day that they would not be able to provide 
17   information about Floyd’s availability until they heard from Floyd himself.  Id.  On February 26, 
18   Defendants indicated that they had “no choice but to issue a notice” for Floyd’s deposition if his 
19   counsel could not provide an available date.  Id. at 4.                   
20        Floyd’s counsel moved for leave to amend the complaint on February 29, seeking to add 
21   two new named plaintiffs but not, at that time, seeking to withdraw Floyd.  Dkt. No. 80.  Apple 
22   opposed that motion on the grounds that Floyd was an improper class representative from the 

23   inception of this case, and that it was unfair that Defendants had been forced to respond to 
24   discovery while this case proceeded with one inadequate named plaintiff.  Dkt. No. 86.  Apple 
1   noted that it had “devoted significant time and expense to discovery, and served requests for 
2   production  and  interrogatories  that  have  been  frustrated  by  Floyd’s  failure  to  respond 
3   substantively.”  Id. at 14.  Defendants argued in the alternative that if new plaintiffs are added, 

4   Floyd’s  counsel  should  be  required  to  show  that  the  Court  should  stay  discovery  against 
5   Defendants to allow them to minimally test whether the new representatives would be adequate 
6   class representatives before requiring Defendants to expend resources on discovery.  Id. at 17–18. 
7        On March 11, 2024, Floyd’s counsel provided “objections and response” to Apple’s 
8   interrogatories (Dkt. No. 90 at 21–28), lodging what Apple characterizes as “boilerplate and 
9   conclusory objections” with no actual information from Floyd, and no indication that the document 
10   was prepared with Floyd’s input or participation.  Dkt. No. 104 at 6.     
11        The Court granted Floyd’s motion for leave to amend on May 6, and Floyd and the new 
12   named Plaintiffs filed a second amended complaint the next day, on May 7.  See Dkt. Nos. 98, 99.  

13   On May 8, Amazon served a notice of Floyd’s deposition on Plaintiffs’ counsel for May 28.  Dkt. 
14   No. 105 at 9.  In that notice, Amazon explained that it “expects that Mr. Floyd will answer 
15   interrogatories and produce responsive documents to Amazon’s outstanding discovery requests … 
16   at least 10 days before the deposition.”  Id.  Plaintiffs’ counsel responded on May 10 that they 
17   would produce Floyd for a deposition if he reengaged with them.  Id. at 20.  Floyd did not reengage, 
18   appear for the deposition, or respond to any of the outstanding discovery requests.   
19        Apple filed this motion to compel Floyd to respond to the discovery requests and appear 
20                                                                             
    for a deposition.  Dkt. No. 104.1  In response/opposition, Plaintiffs’ counsel cross-moved to 
21   withdraw Floyd as a named plaintiff, although Floyd intends to remain an absent class member.  
22   Dkt. No. 114.  In a consolidated reply/response, Apple agrees that Floyd may withdraw as a named 
23                                                                             

24   1 Amazon concurred in the motion as well.  See Dkt. No. 104 at 5 n.1.     
1   plaintiff if he chooses, but insists that his withdrawal should be conditioned on his testifying for a 
2   deposition and responding to the discovery requests that were propounded or noticed while he 
3   remained a named Plaintiff (as he does to this day).  Dkt. No. 125.  Defendants contend that they

10                              II.  ANALYSIS                                  
11        The burden to obtain discovery of any kind from absent class members is very high. See, 
12   e.g., Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts, 472 U.S. 797, 810 n.2 (1985) (noting that burdens, including 
13   discovery, “are rarely imposed upon plaintiff class members”).  On the other hand, by filing a 
14   lawsuit in a putative class action, a named plaintiff is obligated to “participate in discovery and 
15   provide testimony.”  Fraley v. Facebook Inc., No. C 11-1726-LHK (PSG), 2012 WL 555071, at 
16   *3  (N.D.  Cal.  Feb.  21,  2012).    The  scope  of  discovery  is  broad,  restricted  only  to  “any 
17   nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional to the needs 
18   of the case[.]”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1).                                
19        Apple contends that the discovery it seeks to compel from Floyd is relevant to: (1) class-
20   certification issues (whether the new named Plaintiffs are typical and adequate representatives of 
21   class members like Floyd); (2) the merits determination of the relevant market; (3) whether Floyd 
22   is a “core customer” referenced in the operative complaint (Dkt. No. 99 ¶ 91) based on his 

23                                                                             

    2 This order refers to the parties’ briefing using CM/ECF page numbers.   
24                                                                             
1   purchasing behavior; (4) whether Plaintiffs are correct that Apple’s device records are inaccurate 
2   (as they have alleged); and (5) Defendants’ defenses pertaining to the statute of limitations and 
3   whether  the  putative  class  members  suffered  an  antitrust  injury.    Dkt.  No.  125  at  12–14.  

4   Accordingly, Apple requests that Floyd be compelled to respond to the outstanding discovery and 
5   testify at a deposition before he is permitted to withdraw as a named plaintiff.  Dkt. No. 104. 
6        Plaintiffs contend that the discovery Apple seeks to compel has limited relevance, and go 
7   on to argue that even if the discovery was relevant, it is not necessary or proportional to the needs 
8   of the case because there are other named Plaintiffs who are ready and willing to respond to 
9   discovery.  Dkt. No. 127 at 4.  Given that Floyd does not want to continue as a named Plaintiff, 
10   and Defendants do not seek to force him to do so, Plaintiffs argue that discovery responses from 
11   the named Plaintiffs other than Floyd are sufficient for Defendants’ purposes.  Id. at 8. 
12        Discovery conditions are sometimes, but not always, imposed on a withdrawing named 

13   plaintiff.  Compare, e.g., Benanav v. Healthy Paws Pet Ins. LLC, No. 2:20-cv-0421-LK, 2023 WL 
14   5227702, at *9–10 (W.D. Wash. Aug. 15, 2023) (where a named plaintiff sought to dismiss his 
15   claims with prejudice, court conditioned dismissal on his providing discovery responses and sitting 
16   for a two-hour deposition limited to issues unique to him); Gallegos v. Atria Management Co., No. 
17   ED  CV  16-888-JGB  (SPx),  2016  WL  11824850,  at  *5  (C.D.  Cal.  Nov.  14,  2016) 
18   (“[N]otwithstanding  [named  plaintiff’s]  uncertain  status,  the  information  defendants  request 
19   remains relevant.  Although it would not necessarily be proper for defendants to seek such 
20   documents from other putative class members at this point, because [named plaintiff] initiated this 
21   action and was the only named plaintiff until a month ago, it is appropriate for defendants to seek 
22   such documents from her.”); Fraley, 2012 WL 555071, at *3 (requiring an outgoing named 

23   plaintiff to appear for a deposition); with, e.g., In re MGM Resorts Int’l Data Breach Litig., No. 
24   2:20-cv-000376-GMN-NJK, 2024 WL 1440902, at *4 (D. Nev. Apr. 2, 2024) (finding that because 
1   dismissing named plaintiffs without conditions “would not deprive [Defendant] of discovery on 
2   uniquely  situated  class  members”  no  unfair  prejudice  would  result  from  the  unconditional 
3   withdrawal of the named plaintiffs); Doe v. Ariz. Hosp. & Healthcare Ass’n, No. CV 07-1292-

4   PHX-SRB, 2009 WL 1423378, at *14 (D. Ariz. Mar. 19, 2009) (declining to impose dismissal 
5   conditions, finding them “particularly unnecessary in light of the fact that there are currently three 
6   identified class representatives who could be … deposed in her stead”).   
7        The Court finds that based on the circumstances of this case, granting Apple’s motion to 
8   compel before turning to consider Floyd’s motion to withdraw is appropriate.  Defendants’ 
9   discovery requests were served long before Floyd sought to withdraw, and most of them were 
10   propounded when Floyd was the sole named Plaintiff.  The Court is satisfied that the discovery 
11   Apple seeks is relevant to its defenses as well as to some of the issues related to class certification 
12   even if Floyd will not be a named plaintiff at that stage.  See Dkt. No. 131 at 42–48 (Apple’s 

13   arguments regarding the relevance of the Floyd discovery requests with respect to the definition 
14   of the relevant market, whether households with Amazon Prime memberships are “locked in” to 
15   purchasing products from Amazon as alleged in the complaint (see, e.g., Dkt. No. 99 ¶¶ 36, 101, 
16   119), whether an antitrust injury occurred, whether the named Plaintiffs’ claims are typical of the 
17   putative class (that would include Floyd)).                               
18        Apple has further explained how the “limited information” that Defendants have been able 
19   to obtain about Floyd to date confirms that he possesses information relevant to the merits of this 
20   litigation as well as class certification.  See Dkt. No. 131 at 49.  Although Plaintiffs dispute (see, 
21   e.g., id. at 56–59) whether the discovery sought by Defendants will be, ultimately, persuasive as 
22   to any claim or defense of this case, or as to class-certification inquiries, they have not shown that 

23   the information sought does not meet the low threshold of relevance or that it is not proportional 
24                                                                             
1   to the needs of the case.  Under these circumstances, Defendants are entitled to the discovery they 
2   seek from Floyd, before he is permitted to withdraw as a named Plaintiff. 
3        Plaintiffs suggest that discovery conditions are inappropriate based on the posture of this
